Design decision

Sampling parameters are not stored in session state. Streamlit widgets are read on every script run and passed to build_options() per request, which is why a slider change takes effect on the very next message (requirement 8) with no extra plumbing.

3Engine & Integration

How the application talks to Ollama, turns timings into metrics, and degrades gracefully. This layer has no Streamlit imports, so it is tested against a stub server.

3.1 Ollama endpoints used

MethodEndpointClient methodUsed for
GET/api/versionversion() / is_alive()Connection banner
GET/api/tagslist_models()Model selector
GET/api/psrunning_models() / loaded_info()Loaded status, size, context, expiry
POST/api/generatepreload() / unload()Load now / Unload (keep_alive 0)
POST/api/chatchat_stream()Streaming completion with think
Numbers to keep apart

Ollama reports 32.9B parameters and a 262 144-token context for this build (nvfp4 weights), while the model card names it 30B-A3B (about 30B total, about 3B active). The GUI uses the model-card figures for the sparsity caption and the 8192-token window is a runtime choice, not a model limit.

3.2 Streaming and live metrics

moe_demo/engine.py
def stream_answer(client: OllamaClient, model: str, messages: list[dict], options: dict,
                  think: bool | str, keep_alive: str) -> Iterator[LiveUpdate]:
    """Stream a reply and yield LiveUpdate objects; the last one carries exact `final` metrics."""
    start = time.perf_counter()
    first: float | None = None
    content, thinking, chunks = "", "", 0
    for ev in client.chat_stream(model, messages, options=options, think=think, keep_alive=keep_alive):
        now = time.perf_counter()
        if ev.kind in ("content", "thinking"):
            if first is None:
                first = now - start
            chunks += 1
            if ev.kind == "content":
                content += ev.text
            else:
                thinking += ev.text
            gen_time = max(now - start - (first or 0), 1e-6)
            yield LiveUpdate(content, thinking, chunks, now - start, first or 0.0,
                             chunks / gen_time if chunks > 1 else 0.0)
        elif ev.kind == "done":
            wall = now - start
            final = from_stats(ev.stats, ttft=first or wall, wall=wall)
            yield LiveUpdate(content, thinking, chunks, wall, first or wall, final.tokens_per_second, final)

Live tokens/s is chunks per second: Ollama streams roughly one token per chunk, so it is an approximation that is replaced by the exact figure as soon as the done chunk arrives.

moe_demo/metrics.py
def from_stats(stats: dict[str, Any], ttft: float = 0.0, wall: float = 0.0) -> RunMetrics:
    """Build RunMetrics from the `done` chunk of /api/chat."""
    return RunMetrics(
        prompt_tokens=int(stats.get("prompt_eval_count") or 0),
        generated_tokens=int(stats.get("eval_count") or 0),
        load_seconds=(stats.get("load_duration") or 0) / NS,
        prompt_eval_seconds=(stats.get("prompt_eval_duration") or 0) / NS,
        generation_seconds=(stats.get("eval_duration") or 0) / NS,
        total_seconds=(stats.get("total_duration") or 0) / NS,
        ttft_seconds=ttft,
        wall_seconds=wall,
    )

moe_demo/engine.py
def build_options(temperature: float, top_p: float, num_ctx: int, num_predict: int) -> dict:
    """Map UI values to Ollama `options`. These are re-read on every request, so changing a
    slider affects the very next message."""
    if not 0.0 <= temperature <= 2.0:
        raise ValueError("temperature must be within 0..2")
    if not 0.0 < top_p <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError("top_p must be within (0, 1]")
    if num_ctx < 512:
        raise ValueError("num_ctx must be at least 512")
    return {"temperature": temperature, "top_p": top_p, "num_ctx": int(num_ctx),
            "num_predict": int(num_predict)}

def resolve_think(mode: str, category_think: str) -> bool | str:
    """Translate the UI reasoning selector into the value of Ollama's `think` field.

    The model accepts False, True or "medium" (see `ollama show`)."""
    chosen = category_think if mode.startswith("Auto") else mode.lower()
    if chosen == "off":
        return False
    if chosen == "medium":
        return "medium"
    if chosen == "on":
        return True
    raise ValueError(f"unknown reasoning mode: {mode!r}")

3.6 Routing simulation

Measured vs illustrative

Measured: tokens/s, time to first token, response time, load time, prompt and generated tokens, reasoning share. Illustrative: which experts fire. Ollama's API has no field for the router's per-token choices, so router_sim simulates top-6-of-128 routing. The GUI says so next to every heatmap.

moe_demo/router_sim.py
def route_token(token: str, category_key: str) -> list[int]:
    """Return the TOP_K expert ids chosen for one token under the given category."""
    affinity = CATEGORIES[category_key].expert_affinity
    scores = []
    for e in range(N_EXPERTS):
        group_name = EXPERT_GROUPS[group_of(e)]
        scores.append((AFFINITY_STRENGTH * affinity.get(group_name, 0.0) + _noise(token, e), e))
    scores.sort(reverse=True)
    return [e for _, e in scores[:TOP_K]]

def simulate(text: str, category_key: str) -> RoutingResult:
    """Simulate routing of every token of `text` and aggregate the selections."""
    if category_key not in CATEGORIES:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown category: {category_key}")
    tokens = tokenize(text) or ["<empty>"]
    counts = [0] * N_EXPERTS
    for tok in tokens:
        for e in route_token(tok, category_key):
            counts[e] += 1
    total = sum(counts)
    group_totals = [0] * len(EXPERT_GROUPS)
    for e, c in enumerate(counts):
        group_totals[group_of(e)] += c
    share = {EXPERT_GROUPS[i]: group_totals[i] / total for i in range(len(EXPERT_GROUPS))}
    top = sorted(((e, c) for e, c in enumerate(counts) if c), key=lambda x: (-x[1], x[0]))[:10]
    return RoutingResult(category_key, len(tokens), counts, share, top)

Properties verified by unit tests: the result is deterministic (same prompt → same picture), always exactly 6 distinct experts per token inside 0…127, and different categories produce different group profiles.

Chapter 4 of 8

4Expert System

What the application teaches about Mixture-of-Experts, how the five task types differ, and where the line between fact and illustration is drawn.

4.1 The MoE idea

A dense transformer applies every weight to every token. A Mixture-of-Experts layer holds many small feed-forward experts and a router that picks a few per token. Nemotron 3.5 Lightning keeps about 30B parameters of knowledge but computes with about 3B per token: 6 of 128 experts (4.7%).

Hybrid architecture

According to the model card, the network interleaves Mamba-2 state-space layers, MoE layers and a few attention layers; Multi-Token-Prediction heads support speculative decoding. Those facts explain flat per-token cost on long inputs and are summarised in the app's MoE guide.

4.2 Eight expert groups and five task types

To make the idea visible without real router telemetry, the 128 experts are drawn as 8 groups of 16. Each category has an affinity for some groups (0–1). These weights encode a plausible, widely reported tendency (code → symbols and structure, narrative → style and grammar) and are an educational assumption.

Task typeSuggested temp.ReasoningSystem promptKeywords (sample)
✍️ Creative writing1.0offYou are a vivid, original writer. Keep answers under 250 words.story, poem, write a, haiku, lyrics
💻 Coding & technical0.2offYou are a senior software engineer. Reply with concise, correct code and a short explanation.code, python, function, bug, debug
📚 Factual Q&A0.2offYou are a precise encyclopedia. Answer factually and briefly; say so if unsure.who , what is, what are, when did, where is
🧠 Analytical reasoning0.4mediumYou are a careful analyst. Work step by step and state your final answer clearly.why, reason, prove, calculate, puzzle
🗜️ Summarization0.3offYou are an expert editor. Be faithful to the source; add nothing that is not in it.summarize, summarise, summary, tl;dr, tldr

4.4 Why AFFINITY_STRENGTH = 0.5

The strength balances category bias against token-level randomness. At 1.6 one group took about 92 % of the selections, which looks like a hard switch rather than a soft router. 0.5 keeps a clear dominant group while still mixing in others, like real MoE traces. The sweep is recomputed at build time:

4.5 One token, six experts

The same token interval routed under two categories. Highlighted cells are the six selected experts; notice that the coding profile favours rows 0 and 6 (code, structure) while the creative profile favours rows 2 and 4 (narrative, grammar).

4.6 Classifying custom queries

Free-text prompts are assigned to a category by a transparent keyword score (classify()), so custom queries also get an explanation panel. On the 15 built-in examples it picks the intended category 15/15 times. That is a sanity check on curated prompts, not a general accuracy claim; ambiguous prompts fall back to factual, and the sidebar lets the user override the guess.

moe_demo/categories.py
def classify(prompt: str) -> tuple[str, dict[str, int]]:
    """Guess the category of a free-text prompt with a transparent keyword score.

    Returns (category_key, scores). Falls back to 'factual' when nothing matches,
    since it is the most generic Q&A shape.
    """
    text = prompt.lower()
    scores = {k: 0 for k in CATEGORIES}
    for key, cat in CATEGORIES.items():
        for kw in cat.keywords:
            if kw in text:
                scores[key] += 1
    # Structural hints: code fences / long pasted text are strong signals.
    if "```" in prompt or re.search(r"\b(def|class|function|SELECT|import)\b", prompt):
        scores["coding"] += 2
    if len(prompt) > 600:
        scores["summarization"] += 1
    best = max(scores, key=lambda k: scores[k])
    return (best if scores[best] > 0 else "factual"), scores

4.7 Do categories really behave differently? (measured)

What is measurable is how the workload differs: generation length, speed and latency per task type (benchmark in Chapter 7). Reasoning produces by far the most tokens because of the thinking trace; short factual answers finish in about a second.

How to read this

Speed differences between categories are small and partly driven by answer length, sampling and system noise; they are not evidence that different experts run at different speeds. The honest conclusion is: the workload differs per task type (measured), the expert routing picture is a teaching aid (simulated).

            for ln in lines:
                self.wfile.write((json.dumps(ln) + "\n").encode())
                self.wfile.flush()
            return None

5.4 Test run and coverage

Coverage is highest where the logic is: the engine, configuration, metrics, router simulation and UI components are at 100 %. The uncovered lines in app.py are the model Load/Unload buttons, the long-prompt branch and defensive error paths that need a real server in a particular state.

No URL, model name or timeout is hard-coded in the application; everything comes from .env (ignored by git) with .env.example as the documented template.

6.4 Lifecycle scripts

ScriptPurposeBehaviour

scripts/stop.shStop itGraceful shutdown using the pid file

6.5 Using the application

  1. Open the URL and confirm the green Ollama online banner (Figure 2-1).
  2. Click Load now once if the model is not resident; the first request otherwise takes about a minute (Cold start versus warm).
  3. Click any pre-loaded example, or type a question into the chat box.
  4. Read the metric cards and the expert panel while the answer streams (Figure 2-4).
  5. Change temperature, top-p, context window, max tokens or reasoning mode and send the next message; no restart is needed.
  6. Open Compare tasks to put routing profiles and measured speeds side by side (Figure 2-6).

7.2 Cold start versus warm

The first request had to load the model: 41.6 s of loading plus 19.7 s of prompt processing (it also touches every weight once), so the first token arrived after 61 s. Afterwards the model stays resident for the keep-alive time and the first token takes 0.50 s on average.

7.3 Reading the cold run

Prompt-processing speed of the cold run (~3 tok/s) is meaningless as a throughput figure: it includes the one-off cost of paging the weights in. Use the warm numbers and the prefill sweep below instead.

7.4 Prompt processing (prefill)

WordsPrompt tokensPrefill (s)Prefill speed (tok/s)TTFT (s)
2003380.784360.90
80011642.085582.28
200028165.055575.16
400055769.555849.73

Prefill runs at roughly 440–580 tokens/s and grows close to linearly with prompt length, which is why the conversation-history switch matters: each turn re-sends earlier turns (the GUI showed 60 → 395 → 681 prompt tokens over three turns).

7.5 Effect of reasoning mode

ExampleModeGeneratedReasoning charsAnswer charsAnsweredWall (s)tok/s
Logic puzzlemedium204878960no45.145.9
Logic puzzleoff204808308yes41.150.3
Math word problemmedium7911331780yes15.352.8
Math word problemoff47301238yes9.651.9
Trade-off analysismedium20487083297yes43.447.7
Trade-off analysisoff127804835yes30.043.2

Reasoning does not make tokens slower; it makes there more of them (the thinking trace is billed in generated tokens). With thinking on, the Logic puzzle used the entire 2048-token budget and never answered; with it off, the same puzzle was answered in the same budget. Quality of the answers was not graded here, only completion and cost.

7.6 Resource use

MetricValueHow it was measured
Peak Ollama CPU111 %summed ps %CPU of processes named ollama, every 0.5 s
Peak system wired memory25.1 GBvm_stat wired pages; system-wide, includes the OS
Ollama resident set (warm)250–276 MBWeights live in wired GPU memory (MLX), not in the process RSS
Model size reported by Ollama21.14 GB at benchmark time/api/ps (later captures: 22.2–22.7 GB incl. context)
Caveats

Wired memory is a whole-system counter, so the 24–25 GB figure is the model plus everything else the OS keeps wired. RSS of the Ollama process is small because the MLX runner keeps weights in GPU-wired memory. GPU utilisation was not sampled (macOS exposes it only with elevated tools).

7.7 Numbers seen in the GUI

Run in the GUIPrompt tokensGeneratedtok/sTTFT (s)Response (s)Source screenshot
Write a function (coding)6029441.90.17.0903_conversation / 02_coding_run
Micro-story (creative)39522742.20.976.2803_conversation (badge)
Logic puzzle (reasoning), 3rd turn681204860.31.3335.1803_conversation / 07_compare
Logic puzzle (reasoning), fresh session792048102.70.2320.1206_reasoning_trace_limit
Run-to-run variance

The same Logic puzzle (2048 generated tokens each time) ran at 45.9 tok/s in the benchmark, 60.3 tok/s in one GUI session and 102.7 tok/s in another. Single runs on a laptop are noisy (thermal state, other processes, memory pressure, possibly speculative decoding with the MTP heads). The benchmark is therefore n = 1 per cell and the figures are indicative, not a rating of the model; the 15-run mean (46 tok/s) is the steadier number.

7.8 Limits of this measurement

  • One machine, one model build, one run per example (no confidence intervals).
  • Short prompts; long-context behaviour above ~5.6k tokens was not measured.
  • Time to first token in the GUI includes network-free but non-zero Streamlit overhead; the benchmark measures the engine directly.
  • Expert activity is never measured; see Routing simulation.

8.3 Diagnostic commands

shell
curl -s http://localhost:11434/api/version        # is Ollama up?
curl -s http://localhost:11434/api/ps             # is the model resident, how big, which context?
ollama list                                       # is the model installed?

curl -s http://localhost:8501/_stcore/health      # is the GUI up? (prints ok)
tail -n 50 .run/app.log                           # GUI log written by scripts/start.sh
lsof -i :8501 -i :11434                           # who owns the ports?
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q                     # run the whole test suite

8.4 Known limitations

  • No real expert telemetry. Ollama exposes no router output; the heatmap is a deterministic simulation.
  • Category affinities are assumptions chosen to illustrate soft specialisation, not measured from this model.
  • Live tokens/s counts streamed chunks, an approximation until the final figure arrives.
  • Metrics are per request; the Compare table is per browser session and is lost on reload.
  • The keyword classifier is deliberately simple; use the sidebar to force a category.
  • Benchmarks are single-run, single-machine (Limits of this measurement).
